newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan continues efforts to boost pork confidence.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan continues efforts to boost pork confidence.

text.p: Taiwan offered free pork dishes at a large government-run picnic and reopened a zoo that had been shut on concerns over a hog epidemic on Sunday as part of efforts to restore confidence in the pork industry.

The southern Kaohsiung city, whose pork production and prices have been decimated by the foot and mouth disease, gave away three tonnes of pork in the second government-sponsored pork "eat-ins" since news of the epidemic broke on March 20.

Meanwhile, the northern capital city of Taipei announced it would reopen a popular zoo after officials vaccinated all the animals and deemed them safe to come into contact with one of the most likely carriers of the virus -- people.
State-run television showed scores of families happily tucking into free lunch boxes of pig feet, noodles and other succulent pork dishes in the Kaohsiung picnic.
"We have to continue to prove to our public that pork products are safe to eat as long as they are cooked well," a city government official said between bites of sweet and sour pork.

Many Taiwan consumers have not touched pork since March 20, the day the cabinet's Council of Agriculture confirmed finding foot and mouth disease and ordered a ban on exports and massive slaughter and vaccination programme.
The deadly contagion have been detected on more than 1,000 of the island's 25,000 farms, with officials projecting that 886,000 out of the island's 14 million pigs would have to be destroyed.
Farmers and soldiers were slaughtering all hogs -- healthy or otherwise -- at all farms struck by the virus, while all cloven-hoofed livestock were being vaccinated at healthy farms.
Even the zoo was taking no chances, ordering a shutdown on March 25 to vaccinate its animals and protect them from potential virus-carrying tourists.
The zoo said it has finished all the vaccinations and planned to reopen on Monday. But veterinarians urged caution from human visitors.

"Tourists should not feed or touch the animals. We also urge those who have been in contact with pig farms not to visit the zoo for now," Chin Chih-mei, a veterinarian for the zoo, said on state television.

Analysts and officials have said the disease could shave as much as one percentage point off Taiwan's gross domestic product growth in 1997, severely jeopardising the island's current economic recovery.
